newsitem.title: UK: Labour's employment spokeswoman in Lords resigns.
newsitem.headline: Labour's employment spokeswoman in Lords resigns.

text.p: An opposition Labour Party member of Britain's House of Lords resigned on Thursday as spokeswoman on employment after publicly defending a lobbyist involved in sleaze allegations in the ruling Conservative party.

Baroness Muriel Turner of Camden has agreed "it would be inappropriate" for her to remain a spokeswoman in the Lords, said Lord Ivor Seward Richard the party's leader in the upper house of parliament.

It was the first time the Labour Party had become involved in the scandal which has badly damaged the image of the Conservative Party a week before their annual conference and less than seven months before they must call a general election.

In a televison interview Turner defended lobbyist Ian Greer who has been accused of making payments to former Conservative trade minister Neil Hamilton and 23 other members of parliament or their local offices.
"I did firmly believe and still do firmly believe in the innocence of Ian Greer and will continue to support him while I believe that," she told Channel 4 news.
"I am quite certain Ian behaved completely honorably."
Turner is a director of Greer's company.
In a statement released quickly after the interview Richard said: "There is no suggestion that she has acted improperly in her capacity as a director of his company."
Labour, which on Friday will finish its last annual conference before the election, was quick to limit any potential damage.

Labour homes affairs spokesman Jack Straw said he agreed with Turner's decision to step down but insisted that her resignation was a "wholly different order of things" than the allegations against Hamilton.

Hamilton resigned as trade minister in 1994 after he was accused of accepting money from Mohammed al-Fayed, the Egyptian-born owner of London's luxury Harrods store, in return for tabling questions in parliament.
He has admitted he accepted two payments totalling 10,000 pounds ($15,600) from Greer in the late 1980s, but has insisted that the money was paid to him for introducing clients to the lobbyist.
Both he and Greer pulled out of a libel case against the Guardian newspaper which published the allegations hours before it was due to start on Tuesday.
Prime Minister John Major has agreed to cooperate fully with an investigation into the claims which will be conducted by parliament's Commissioner For Standards Sir Gordon Downey.
